introduction_markdown:
**Cameroon General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. History 3 (0760), Paper 3 - Africa and World History, ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2026. Duration: three hours.**

Instructions to candidates: Candidates are required to answer FOUR questions, choosing ONE from each of the four sections (Section A: Africa, 1800-1945; Section B: Africa, 1945 to the present; Section C: World Revolutions and Diplomacy, 1700-1919; Section D: World, 1919 to the present date). All questions carry equal marks (25 marks each).

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.
incertitudes: Aucun corrigé officiel n'existe : les réponses modèles sont rédigées (introduction, développement, conclusion) à partir de l'historiographie courante ; en cas de doute sur une date ou un fait, la formulation est prudente ou le détail est omis.

Règle de choix de la page de garde : « answer FOUR questions, choosing ONE from each of the four sections » ; elle est exprimée par une règle « 1 sur 3 » par section (A à D), identique dans les 12 fichiers. Le sujet laisse donc exactement une question par section.

Le sujet imprime « (25 marks) » après chaque question et « All questions carry equal marks » ; les points ne sont pas corrigés. Aucune figure ni document dans le sujet (2 pages : page de garde et questions).

Question 1 : dates de l'historiographie courante (Danemark 1803, loi britannique de 1807, loi américaine entrée en vigueur en 1808, escadron britannique d'Afrique de l'Ouest à partir de 1808, déclaration du Congrès de Vienne en 1815, abolition de l'esclavage dans l'Empire britannique en 1833, Liberia 1822, traité de Bimbia en 1840, bombardement de Lagos en 1851, annexion en 1861). L'implication des traités avec les chefs côtiers du Cameroun (Bimbia, Douala) est formulée prudemment, sans détail de signataires. Aucun chiffre sur le nombre de captifs avancé.

questions.enonce_markdown:
What factors made the abolition of slave trade in West Africa in the 19th century inevitable?

(25 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** The Trans-Atlantic slave trade had been the main link between West Africa and the outside world for about three centuries. In the 19th century, however, it was attacked from many sides and was finally brought to an end in the Atlantic. To say that abolition was "inevitable" means that several powerful forces, humanitarian, economic, political, military and even African, were working together in the same direction so that the trade could not survive. No single cause was enough: it was their combination that made abolition certain.

**1. Humanitarian and religious factors.**
- Evangelical Christians and Quakers condemned slavery as a sin against God and humanity. Campaigners such as Granville Sharp, Thomas Clarkson and William Wilberforce, helped by the Clapham Sect and by the writing of ex-slaves such as Olaudah Equiano, used petitions, pamphlets, public meetings and boycotts of slave-grown sugar to win public opinion.
- Enlightenment thinkers argued that all men have natural rights. The court decision in the Somerset case (1772) in England and the example of the Haitian Revolution (1791-1804), in which slaves defeated their masters, made the moral argument stronger and made slave owners fear revolts.
- The result was Denmark's ban (effective 1803), the British Slave Trade Act of 1807, the American ban on importing slaves (effective 1808) and, at the Congress of Vienna (1815), a declaration by the powers that the trade should be ended. Britain used its diplomatic influence to make other nations follow.

**2. Economic factors.**
- The Industrial Revolution created a need for raw materials such as palm oil (used for soap and for lubricating machines), groundnuts and later cotton, and for markets for British manufactured goods. This was possible only if West African producers stayed in Africa and produced goods instead of being shipped away. "Legitimate commerce" was therefore seen as more profitable than slaving.
- Economists such as Adam Smith argued that free labour was more productive than slave labour. The West Indian sugar economy was in relative decline by the early 19th century, so the planters' lobby in Parliament lost strength. Historians such as Eric Williams (Capitalism and Slavery, 1944) stressed these economic changes, although other historians insist that humanitarian pressure was also decisive.

**3. Political and military factors.**
- Britain, then the strongest naval power, created the West Africa Squadron (from 1808) based at Freetown, which captured slave ships and freed captives. It signed anti-slave trade treaties with Portugal, Spain, France, the Netherlands and later with Brazil, and with African rulers (for example the coastal rulers of the Bight of Biafra and the Cameroon coast, such as Bimbia in 1840). Where a ruler refused, force was used: Lagos was bombarded in 1851 and annexed in 1861 as part of the effort to end the trade.
- Freetown became a haven of freed slaves (Sierra Leone became a Crown colony in 1808), and the American Colonization Society founded Liberia (1822), both of which served as bases against the trade and for Christian and commercial influence.
- Abolition of slavery itself in the British Empire (1833, effective 1834) and in French colonies (1848) removed the main markets and the moral justification of the trade.

**4. The role of missionaries, explorers and Africans.** Missionaries (the Church Missionary Society, Methodists, Baptists) and explorers (Mungo Park, Clapperton, the Lander brothers, the Niger expedition of 1841) reported the horrors of the trade, and promoted Christianity, commerce and civilisation, as Thomas Fowell Buxton argued. Some African rulers and merchants, such as many coastal middlemen, switched to the new trade in palm oil, and so the economic basis of the old system weakened, although others resisted, for example some powerful states that depended on the profits of the trade, and these were forced to adapt.

**Conclusion.** The abolition of the slave trade in West Africa was inevitable because moral conviction, economic self-interest, naval power and the changing economy of both Europe and Africa pushed in the same direction. Humanitarians gave the movement its moral strength, industrial capitalism gave it economic logic, and the British navy and treaties gave it the means. Once these forces joined, the Atlantic slave trade could only decline, although the trade continued illegally for some decades and slavery within Africa itself even increased as African producers used slave labour on plantations of palm oil and other crops.
